\section*{Derivative Notation Guide}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}p{.25\textwidth}X@{}}
\toprule
Notation&Meaning\\\midrule
\(f'(a)\)&derivative value at the particular input \(a\)\\
\(f'(x)\)&derivative function\\
\(y'\)&derivative of \(y\) with respect to the understood input\\
\(dy/dx\)&derivative of \(y\) with respect to \(x\)\\
\(d/dx[f(x)]\)&operator notation: differentiate the bracketed function\\
\(f''(x)\), \(d^2y/dx^2\)&second derivative\\
\(f^{(n)}(x)\)&\(n\)th derivative\\
\(\dot s\), \(\ddot s\)&first and second time derivatives\\
\(\partial f/\partial x\)&partial derivative, reserved for multivariable calculus\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

The symbols look different because mathematicians needed notation suited to different tasks. Prime notation is compact. Leibniz notation makes the input variable visible and works especially well in chain-rule and applied calculations. Operator notation clearly identifies what is being differentiated.

\begin{bgtranslation}[title={Read before manipulating}]
\[
\frac{d}{dx}[x^3+1]
\]
means ``differentiate the entire bracketed function with respect to \(x\).'' It is an instruction, not a fraction waiting to cancel with an \(x\).
\end{bgtranslation}

\chapter{The Derivative as an Instantaneous Rate}
\section{From an Interval to an Instant}
\lessonobjective{Explain why an instantaneous rate must be defined by a limit; connect average rate, secant slope, instantaneous rate, and tangent slope.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
Read \emph{Why Derivatives Matter} as a lesson in translation rather than notation. The derivative can be described in words as an instantaneous rate, in geometry as a tangent slope, in a table as the limiting trend of secant slopes, and in symbols as a limit. None of these viewpoints is secondary; each becomes useful in a different kind of problem.

Before calculating, say what a positive, zero, or negative answer would mean. That prediction gives you a built-in error check. A rising graph should not produce a negative tangent slope, and a cost derivative should not be reported without cost-per-unit units. The meaning is part of the mathematics, not commentary added afterward.
\end{bgexposition}



The derivative is the mathematical instrument for answering ``how fast, how steep, or how sensitive right now?'' Average change compares two snapshots. A derivative asks what remains when the snapshots are squeezed together until they describe one instant. That limiting process turns a familiar slope calculation into a tool for motion, growth, economics, medicine, engineering, and any other subject where one quantity responds to another.

Do not reduce the derivative to a bag of formulas. A formula such as \(f'(x)=3x^2\) is useful because it tells a story: near input \(x\), a small input change \(\Delta x\) produces an output change of about \(3x^2\Delta x\). The entire unit develops ways to compute that local response and then use it intelligently.

A speedometer reports a speed at one instant, but speed is computed by comparing changes in position and time. This creates the first puzzle of differential calculus: a single instant has no elapsed time. Dividing a change in position by zero seconds is impossible.

The solution is not to invent a tiny magical time interval. We use ordinary nonzero intervals, compute ordinary average rates, and examine what those rates approach as the intervals shrink.

For a function \(f\), the average rate of change from \(x=a\) to \(x=a+h\) is
\[
\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h},\qquad h\ne0.
\]
This is the slope of the secant line through \((a,f(a))\) and \((a+h,f(a+h))\). If the slopes approach one finite number as \(h\to0\), that number is the derivative at \(a\).

\begin{bgconcept}[title={The simplest mental picture}]
A secant line uses two points on a curve. A tangent line records the direction of the curve at one point. The derivative is the number obtained when the second secant point slides toward the first and the secant slopes settle toward a limit.
\end{bgconcept}

\begin{bgguided}[title={Instantaneous velocity from a shrinking interval}]
A particle has position
\[
s(t)=t^2+3t
\]
in meters after \(t\) seconds. Find its instantaneous velocity at \(t=2\).

\begin{bgsolution}
We cannot compare \(t=2\) with itself because the elapsed time would be zero. Compare \(2\) with \(2+h\), where \(h\ne0\):
\[
\frac{s(2+h)-s(2)}{h}.
\]
First calculate each position:
\[
s(2)=2^2+3(2)=10,
\]
\[
\begin{aligned}
s(2+h)&=(2+h)^2+3(2+h)\\
&=4+4h+h^2+6+3h\\
&=10+7h+h^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Subtract the starting position:
\[
s(2+h)-s(2)=7h+h^2.
\]
Divide by the elapsed time \(h\):
\[
\frac{7h+h^2}{h}=7+h,\qquad h\ne0.
\]
Now let the nonzero interval shrink:
\[
\lim_{h\to0}(7+h)=7.
\]
Therefore the instantaneous velocity is
\[
\boxed{7\text{ m/s}}.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgeditorialvisual}[title={Existing visual 2A-E01 - secant lines converging to a tangent}]
\textbf{Purpose and placement.} This is the first quantitative graph in Unit 2A and should remain near the initial shrinking-interval example. Its job is to show that an instantaneous rate is obtained from a family of ordinary secant slopes rather than from dividing by a zero-length interval. The student should be able to connect each colored line to one nonzero value of $h$ and see the tangent as the limiting line.

\textbf{Exact composition.} Plot $s(t)=t^2+3t$ with the fixed point $P=(2,10)$. The red secants correspond to sample second points and should be visibly distinct from the final green tangent. The tangent equation is $s-10=7(t-2)$. Preserve the grid and units-oriented axis labels. In the revised web figure, include the moving point $Q=(2+h,s(2+h))$, a horizontal readout for $h$, and the computed secant slope $7+h$.

\textbf{Interaction.} The learner should drag $Q$ from either side of $P$. As $Q$ approaches $P$, update the secant equation and slope. A step mode should offer $h=1,0.5,0.1,0.01,-0.01$ before free dragging.

\textbf{Accessibility and responsive behavior.} Alt text should name the function, fixed point, representative secants, and limiting tangent slope. Use line pattern as well as color. On mobile, place slope and $h$ readouts below the graph. The interactive point must be keyboard movable.
\end{bgeditorialvisual}

\begin{bgcheck}{deriv-foundation-01}{integer}{12}[Quick check]
For \(f(x)=x^2\), evaluate
\[
\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(6+h)-f(6)}{h}.
\]
\begin{bghint}Expand \((6+h)^2\), subtract \(36\), then divide every term by \(h\).\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}
\[
\frac{(6+h)^2-36}{h}=\frac{12h+h^2}{h}=12+h\to\boxed{12}.
\]
\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}


\begin{bgapplication}[title={A medication level is rising, but is it rising safely?}]
A simplified concentration model is
\[
C(t)=12t-1.5t^2
\]
for the first four hours after a dose, with \(C\) measured in milligrams per liter. The average concentration change from hour \(1\) to hour \(3\) is
\[
\frac{C(3)-C(1)}{3-1}=6\text{ mg/L per hour}.
\]
The instantaneous rate at \(t=1\) comes from the derivative and equals \(9\) mg/L per hour, while at \(t=3\) it equals \(3\) mg/L per hour. The concentration is still increasing at both times, but the increase is slowing. This distinction between amount and rate is precisely why derivatives matter in applications.
\end{bgapplication}

\section{The Formal Definition at a Point}
\lessonobjective{Use the limit definition to calculate \(f'(a)\); interpret the result as a rate and a tangent slope.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The main idea behind \emph{The Derivative at a Point} is local change. A graph may be complicated over a large interval and still behave in a simple, nearly linear way near one input. The derivative records that local direction. It does not describe the total amount of the function, and it does not automatically describe what happens far from the point.

Use three representations whenever possible: a numerical rate from nearby values, a slope on a graph, and a symbolic limit or derivative. When all three tell the same story, the calculation is much easier to trust. When they disagree, the disagreement usually exposes a dropped sign, a misread unit, or a function that is not differentiable at the point.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoALocalLinearity



At a single point, the graph does not provide two distinct points from which to calculate a slope. The derivative solves that problem by using nearby secant slopes and asking whether they settle toward one number. The resulting value belongs to one input, so \(f'(a)\) is a number, not yet a new formula.

This lesson is worth doing slowly. Once the difference quotient has been simplified correctly, the limit is often easy. Most errors happen earlier: parentheses are dropped, a common factor is not exposed, or \(f(a+h)\) is evaluated as though the \(+h\) were decorative.

\begin{bgdefinition}[title={Derivative at a point}]
Let \(f\) be defined near \(x=a\). The derivative of \(f\) at \(a\) is
\[
\boxed{f'(a)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}},
\]
provided the limit exists as a finite real number.
\end{bgdefinition}

The derivative has three equivalent interpretations:
\begin{enumerate}
\item the instantaneous rate of change of \(f\) with respect to \(x\) at \(a\);
\item the limiting value of average rates on intervals shrinking toward \(a\);
\item the slope of the tangent line to \(y=f(x)\) at \((a,f(a))\).
\end{enumerate}

\begin{bgguided}[title={Derivative of a quadratic at one point}]
Use the limit definition to find the derivative of
\[
f(x)=x^2-4x+1
\]
at \(x=3\).

\begin{bgsolution}
Start with the definition:
\[
f'(3)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(3+h)-f(3)}{h}.
\]
Calculate \(f(3)\):
\[
f(3)=9-12+1=-2.
\]
Now calculate \(f(3+h)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(3+h)&=(3+h)^2-4(3+h)+1\\
&=9+6h+h^2-12-4h+1\\
&=-2+2h+h^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Form the difference quotient:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{f(3+h)-f(3)}{h}
&=\frac{(-2+2h+h^2)-(-2)}{h}\\
&=\frac{2h+h^2}{h}\\
&=2+h.
\end{aligned}
\]
Take the limit:
\[
f'(3)=\lim_{h\to0}(2+h)=\boxed{2}.
\]
The graph has tangent slope \(2\) at \((3,-2)\). Since the output has no physical units in this example, the derivative is simply two output units per input unit.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={A reciprocal function from first principles}]
Find \(f'(2)\) for \(f(x)=1/x\).
\begin{bgsolution}
\[
\begin{aligned}
f'(2)
&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\frac1{2+h}-\frac12}{h}\\
&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\frac{2-(2+h)}{2(2+h)}}{h}\\
&=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{-h}{2(2+h)h}\\
&=\lim_{h\to0}-\frac1{2(2+h)}\\
&=\boxed{-\frac14}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The negative sign matches the graph: \(1/x\) is decreasing near \(x=2\).
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgmistake}
The symbol \(h\) is not the derivative. It is the change in the input. The derivative is the limit of the entire quotient as \(h\to0\). Cancelling a factor of \(h\) is permitted only after algebra reveals that factor and only because the quotient is studied for \(h\ne0\).
\end{bgmistake}

\begin{bgexercises}
\item Use the definition to find \(f'(1)\) for \(f(x)=x^2+2x\).
\item Use the definition to find \(g'(-1)\) for \(g(x)=3x^2-x\).
\item Use the definition to find \(p'(4)\) for \(p(x)=\sqrt{x}\). Rationalize the numerator.
\item Explain in one sentence what \(C'(100)=4.25\) means if \(C(q)\) is production cost in dollars for \(q\) units.
\end{bgexercises}


\begin{bgadvanced}[title={Analysis preview: differentiability is an error statement}]
In a later real-analysis course, the derivative is often expressed by
\[
f(a+h)=f(a)+f'(a)h+r(h),
\qquad
\frac{r(h)}{h}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The remainder \(r(h)\) may not be zero, but it becomes negligible compared with \(h\). This formulation says more than ``the tangent slope exists'': it says the tangent line captures the entire first-order behavior of the function. The derivative is therefore the coefficient of the best local linear model.
\end{bgadvanced}

\section{An Algebra Clinic for the Limit Definition}
\lessonobjective{Evaluate \(f(a+h)\) correctly, preserve parentheses, expose a factor of \(h\), and explain why cancellation is legal.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The main idea behind \emph{Difference Quotient Algebra Without Skipped Steps} is local change. A graph may be complicated over a large interval and still behave in a simple, nearly linear way near one input. The derivative records that local direction. It does not describe the total amount of the function, and it does not automatically describe what happens far from the point.

Use three representations whenever possible: a numerical rate from nearby values, a slope on a graph, and a symbolic limit or derivative. When all three tell the same story, the calculation is much easier to trust. When they disagree, the disagreement usually exposes a dropped sign, a misread unit, or a function that is not differentiable at the point.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoADifferenceQuotient


The derivative definition is conceptually simple and algebraically unforgiving. Most first-principles errors occur before the limit: a student substitutes \(a+h\) into only one occurrence of \(x\), forgets parentheses around \(f(a)\), or cancels an \(h\) that is not a factor of every numerator term.

\begin{bgtranslation}[title={What \(f(a+h)\) means}]
Replace every free occurrence of the input variable by the complete expression \(a+h\). If \(f(x)=3x^2-2x+4\), then
\[
f(a+h)=3(a+h)^2-2(a+h)+4,
\]
not \(3a+h^2-2a+h+4\) and not \(3(a+h)^2-2a+4\).
\end{bgtranslation}

\begin{bgguided}[title={A full difference quotient with every algebra decision visible}]
Let \(f(x)=2x^2-3x\). Simplify
\[
\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}.
\]
\begin{bgsolution}
First calculate the shifted output:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(a+h)
&=2(a+h)^2-3(a+h)\\
&=2(a^2+2ah+h^2)-3a-3h\\
&=2a^2+4ah+2h^2-3a-3h.
\end{aligned}
\]
Now calculate the unshifted output:
\[
f(a)=2a^2-3a.
\]
Subtract the entire quantity \(f(a)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(a+h)-f(a)
&=2a^2+4ah+2h^2-3a-3h-(2a^2-3a)\\
&=4ah+2h^2-3h.
\end{aligned}
\]
Every remaining term contains a factor of \(h\):
\[
4ah+2h^2-3h=h(4a+2h-3).
\]
Since the difference quotient is formed for \(h\ne0\), cancel the common factor:
\[
\frac{h(4a+2h-3)}{h}=4a+2h-3.
\]
Therefore the limiting value as \(h\to0\) is \(4a-3\).
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgmistake}[title={Cancellation is about factors, not matching symbols}]
In \((h+2)/h\), the \(h\) in the denominator does not cancel with the \(h\) inside the sum. Cancellation is division by a common factor of the entire numerator and denominator. Factoring is the step that makes the common factor visible.
\end{bgmistake}

\begin{bgcheck}{difference-quotient-01}{expression}{2a+1}[Quick check]
For \(g(x)=x^2+x\), simplify the difference quotient and then let \(h\to0\).
\begin{bghint}Expand \((a+h)^2+(a+h)\), subtract \(a^2+a\), and factor \(h\).\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}
\[
\frac{g(a+h)-g(a)}h
=\frac{2ah+h^2+h}{h}=2a+h+1\to\boxed{2a+1}.
\]
\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}

\section{Equations of Tangent and Normal Lines}
\lessonobjective{Use a derivative value and a point on a curve to write tangent and normal line equations.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The main idea behind \emph{Tangent and Normal Lines} is local change. A graph may be complicated over a large interval and still behave in a simple, nearly linear way near one input. The derivative records that local direction. It does not describe the total amount of the function, and it does not automatically describe what happens far from the point.

Use three representations whenever possible: a numerical rate from nearby values, a slope on a graph, and a symbolic limit or derivative. When all three tell the same story, the calculation is much easier to trust. When they disagree, the disagreement usually exposes a dropped sign, a misread unit, or a function that is not differentiable at the point.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoATangentNormal



A derivative gives a slope, but a slope alone is not a line. To build the tangent line, pair the derivative value with the point of tangency. The result is the line that best matches the curve near that point, which is why tangent lines later become approximation machines rather than merely geometry exercises.

Normal lines are perpendicular to tangent lines. They matter in geometric design, optics, and surface modeling, but the same algebraic warning applies: a zero tangent slope produces a vertical normal line, so the negative-reciprocal shortcut must be interpreted rather than applied mechanically.

Once \(f'(a)\) is known, the tangent line passes through \((a,f(a))\) with slope \(f'(a)\). Point-slope form gives
\[
\boxed{y-f(a)=f'(a)(x-a)}.
\]
A normal line is perpendicular to the tangent line. If \(f'(a)\ne0\), its slope is
\[
-\frac1{f'(a)}.
\]
If the tangent is horizontal, the normal is vertical. If the tangent is vertical, the normal is horizontal.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Write a tangent line without skipping the point}]
Let \(f(x)=x^2-4x+1\). The previous lesson found \(f'(3)=2\). Find the tangent line at \(x=3\).
\begin{bgsolution}
The slope is already known:
\[
m=f'(3)=2.
\]
We still need the point. The input is \(3\), and
\[
f(3)=-2.
\]
So the tangent point is \((3,-2)\). Substitute into point-slope form:
\[
y-(-2)=2(x-3).
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{y+2=2(x-3)}
\]
or, after simplification,
\[
\boxed{y=2x-8}.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={Tangent and normal lines to a reciprocal curve}]
For \(f(x)=1/x\), find the tangent and normal lines at \(x=2\).
\begin{bgsolution}
The point is \((2,1/2)\), and the derivative value from the previous page is \(-1/4\). Thus the tangent line is
\[
\boxed{y-\frac12=-\frac14(x-2)}.
\]
The normal slope is the negative reciprocal of \(-1/4\), namely \(4\). Therefore the normal line is
\[
\boxed{y-\frac12=4(x-2)}.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgcheck}{tangent-line-01}{expression}{y=6x-9}[Quick check]
Find the tangent line to \(f(x)=x^2\) at \(x=3\).
\begin{bghint}The point is \((3,9)\), and the derivative slope is \(2(3)=6\).\end{bghint}
\begin{bgreveal}
\[
y-9=6(x-3),
\]
so \(\boxed{y=6x-9}\). The web checker should accept equivalent point-slope and slope-intercept forms.
\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}
\begin{bgmistake}[title={Do not confuse the input with the point}]
At \(x=a\), the tangent point is \((a,f(a))\), not \((a,a)\). A large fraction of tangent-line errors are not calculus errors at all; they are failures to calculate the output coordinate.
\end{bgmistake}


\begin{bgmodelinglab}[title={Road grade from an elevation model}]
A trail's elevation in meters is modeled near kilometer marker \(x=2\) by
\[
E(x)=120+18x-2x^2.
\]
Then
\[
E'(x)=18-4x,
\qquad E'(2)=10.
\]
The tangent-line model is
\[
L(x)=E(2)+10(x-2)=148+10(x-2).
\]
Thus, near marker \(2\), every additional kilometer raises elevation by about \(10\) meters. The local grade as a decimal is \(10/1000=0.01\), or about \(1\%\).
\end{bgmodelinglab}

\section{Notation, Units, and Meaning}
\lessonobjective{Translate among common derivative notations and state derivative units correctly.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The symbols in \emph{Derivative Notation and Units} compress three different questions: what the function value is, how two values compare, and what the comparison approaches when the inputs merge. Keep those questions separate. Most confusion at the beginning of differential calculus comes from treating an instantaneous rate as if it were an ordinary quotient over zero distance or zero time. It is not. It is a limit of ordinary quotients over nonzero intervals.

As you work, translate every expression into a sentence. Identify the input, the output, the point of interest, and the units. Then decide whether the problem is asking for a number at one point, a formula for all points, or a line that represents local behavior. This slower reading habit quickly becomes faster than trying to repair symbol errors after several lines of algebra.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoANotationUnits



Derivative notation looks crowded because it was invented by several mathematicians for different purposes. The notations are not rival answers. They emphasize different features: \(f'(a)\) highlights evaluation, \(dy/dx\) highlights which variable changes with respect to which, and \(d/dx\) acts as an instruction.

Units are not optional decoration. If \(C(q)\) is cost in dollars for producing \(q\) items, then \(C'(q)\) has units dollars per item. Those units reveal what the derivative means and frequently expose nonsense before an answer reaches the grader.

The same derivative may be written in several ways:
\[
f'(x),\qquad y',\qquad \frac{dy}{dx},\qquad \frac{d}{dx}[f(x)],\qquad D_xf(x).
\]
If the independent variable is time, dots are common in physics:
\[
\dot{s}(t)=\frac{ds}{dt},\qquad \ddot{s}(t)=\frac{d^2s}{dt^2}.
\]

Leibniz notation is especially useful when variables and units matter. If \(V(r)\) is volume in cubic centimeters and \(r\) is radius in centimeters, then
\[
\frac{dV}{dr}
\]
has units
\[
\frac{\text{cubic centimeters}}{\text{centimeter}}.
\]
Do not simplify units so aggressively that their meaning disappears.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Interpret a derivative in context}]
Suppose \(T(d)\) is soil temperature in degrees Celsius at depth \(d\) meters, and
\[
T'(12)=0.018.
\]
Explain the meaning.
\begin{bgsolution}
The input is depth and the output is temperature. Therefore the derivative units are degrees Celsius per meter. At a depth of \(12\) meters, temperature is increasing with depth at an instantaneous rate of about
\[
\boxed{0.018\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}/\mathrm{m}}.
\]
For a small additional depth of one meter near \(d=12\), the temperature should increase by approximately \(0.018^\circ\mathrm C\).
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={Marginal cost}]
If \(C(q)\) is the cost in dollars of producing \(q\) items and \(C'(500)=7.30\), then at a production level of 500 items, cost is increasing at about \(\$7.30\) per additional item. The derivative is not the total cost of item 500; it is a local rate and an approximation to the cost of the next item.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgcheck}{units-derivative-01}{text}{liters per centimeter}[Quick check]
A tank contains \(W(h)\) liters of water when the depth is \(h\) centimeters. What are the units of \(W'(h)\)?
\begin{bgreveal}The output is measured in liters and the input in centimeters, so the units are \(\boxed{\text{liters per centimeter}}\).\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}


\begin{bgapplication}[title={Battery discharge rate}]
Let \(Q(t)\) be battery charge in watt-hours after \(t\) hours of use. If
\[
Q'(2)=-18,
\]
then at hour \(2\) the battery is losing charge at \(18\) watt-hours per hour. The negative sign describes decreasing charge; it does not make the physical discharge rate ``negative'' in ordinary language. One might report: ``the charge is decreasing at \(18\) Wh/h.''
\end{bgapplication}

\chapter{The Core Differentiation Rules}
\section{Constants, Powers, Sums, and Differences}
\lessonobjective{Differentiate constants and power functions; use constant multiples, sums, and differences; distinguish a coefficient from an exponent.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
In \emph{The Constant and Power Rules}, the challenge is not remembering a longer formula list. It is seeing how an expression was built. Differentiation rules mirror construction rules: sums are handled term by term, products require two contributions, quotients balance numerator and denominator change, and compositions require the chain rule. The outermost operation determines the first move.

Write a one-line rule plan before doing algebra. For example, label an expression ``product outside, chain rule in the second factor.'' This takes seconds and prevents the most expensive errors. Keep grouping visible until the derivative structure is complete; simplify only when simplification makes the next decision clearer.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoAPowerRuleFamily




\begin{bgexposition}[title={The exponent moves because the local change has one fewer factor}]
The power rule can look like a trick: bring the exponent down and subtract one. Its origin is less magical. Expanding \((x+h)^n\) produces a leading change term \(nx^{n-1}h\); after division by \(h\), the coefficient \(nx^{n-1}\) remains while higher powers of \(h\) vanish in the limit.

When using the rule, rewrite radicals and reciprocals as powers first. That single habit turns many apparently different formulas into the same pattern and makes sign errors easier to catch.
\end{bgexposition}

The power rule compresses a limit calculation into a two-move pattern: multiply by the exponent and lower that exponent by one. The pattern is simple, but it represents a profound fact about how scaling laws respond to change. Area grows like length squared, volume like length cubed, and their derivatives reveal how quickly those quantities become more sensitive as size increases.

Use the rule term by term, and keep coefficients separate from exponents. The derivative operator is linear, so a polynomial can be dismantled, differentiated in pieces, and reassembled without changing the result.

The limit definition explains what a derivative means. Differentiation rules make routine computation efficient. The rules are not replacements for the definition; they are results proved from it.

\begin{bgtheorem}[title={Constant and power rules}]
For a constant \(c\),
\[
\frac{d}{dx}[c]=0.
\]
For any real exponent \(n\) on an interval where \(x^n\) is defined and differentiable,
\[
\boxed{\frac{d}{dx}[x^n]=nx^{n-1}}.
\]
\end{bgtheorem}

A constant function has a horizontal graph, so its slope is zero. The power rule performs two visible moves: multiply by the old exponent, then reduce the exponent by one.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Use the power rule one term at a time}]
Differentiate
\[
f(x)=4x^5-3x^2+7x-9.
\]
\begin{bgsolution}
Differentiate each term independently:
\[
\frac{d}{dx}[4x^5]=4\cdot5x^4=20x^4,
\]
\[
\frac{d}{dx}[-3x^2]=-3\cdot2x=-6x,
\]
\[
\frac{d}{dx}[7x]=7,
\]
\[
\frac{d}{dx}[-9]=0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{f'(x)=20x^4-6x+7}.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgproofidea}[title={Why the integer power rule has this shape}]
For \(f(x)=x^n\),
\[
\frac{(x+h)^n-x^n}{h}.
\]
The binomial expansion begins
\[
(x+h)^n=x^n+nx^{n-1}h+\binom n2x^{n-2}h^2+\cdots+h^n.
\]
After subtracting \(x^n\) and dividing by \(h\), the first surviving term is \(nx^{n-1}\); every other term still contains a positive power of \(h\) and vanishes as \(h\to0\).
\end{bgproofidea}

\begin{bgmistake}
For \(5x^3\), the derivative is \(15x^2\), not \(5x^2\) and not \(3x^2\). The coefficient stays and the exponent comes down as an additional factor.
\end{bgmistake}

\begin{bgcheck}{power-rule-01}{expression}{18x^5-8x^3+2}[Quick check]
Differentiate \(3x^6-2x^4+2x-11\).
\begin{bgreveal}\(\boxed{18x^5-8x^3+2}\).\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}


\begin{bgapplication}[title={Why larger spheres gain volume so quickly}]
The volume of a sphere is \(V(r)=\frac43\pi r^3\). Differentiating with respect to radius gives
\[
V'(r)=4\pi r^2.
\]
At \(r=2\), adding a small \(0.01\) unit to the radius increases volume by approximately
\[
V'(2)(0.01)=16\pi(0.01)\approx0.503.
\]
At \(r=10\), the same radial increase produces about \(4\pi\) cubic units. Sensitivity grows with surface area, which is not a coincidence: a thin outer shell has volume approximately surface area times thickness.
\end{bgapplication}

\begin{bgadvanced}[title={Beyond integer powers}]
The binomial proof directly handles positive integers. Extending the power rule to negative integers, rational exponents, and arbitrary real exponents requires additional arguments and careful domains. One route writes \(x^r=e^{r\ln x}\) for \(x>0\) and uses the chain rule. The familiar formula survives, but its proof depends on the theory of exponential and logarithmic functions.
\end{bgadvanced}

\section{From Repeated Limit Work to Reusable Rules}
\lessonobjective{Explain how derivative rules compress repeated limit arguments and distinguish a rule from the definition it summarizes.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The shortcuts in \emph{Derivative Rules Are Shortcuts, Not New Definitions} do not replace the limit definition. They package conclusions already justified from it. That distinction matters because a rule applies only when the function has the relevant structure and lies in its domain. A familiar-looking exponent or fraction is not permission to differentiate blindly.

After using a rule, check the result structurally. A derivative of a polynomial should have lower degree. A product derivative should usually contain contributions from both factors. A quotient result should preserve the denominator restriction. These checks are quick enough to use on homework and valuable enough to use on exams.
\end{bgexposition}



\begin{bgexposition}[title={Shortcuts are compressed proofs}]
A differentiation rule is not a new definition competing with the limit definition. It is a theorem proved from that definition. Once the theorem is established, using it is no more dishonest than using the distributive law instead of re-proving it every time you multiply.

Knowing this matters when a rule seems to fail. The failure usually comes from misreading the function's structure, not from a defect in calculus. Returning to the limit definition or to the rule's proof reveals which assumption or algebraic pattern was overlooked.
\end{bgexposition}

The limit definition remains the foundation of every derivative. The computation rules do not replace that definition; they package conclusions that have already been proved. Once the power rule tells us
\[
\frac{d}{dx}x^n=nx^{n-1},
\]
we no longer expand \((x+h)^n\) from scratch each time. We use the theorem and save our attention for structure, algebra, and interpretation.

\begin{bgconcept}[title={Rules reduce repetition, not understanding}]
Using the power rule is no more dishonest than using multiplication instead of repeated addition. The important question is whether you know when the rule applies and what assumptions it carries.
\end{bgconcept}

\begin{bgcheckpoint}[title={Rule-recognition warm-up}]
For each expression, name the outer structure before differentiating:
\[
5x^4-3x,
\qquad
x^2\sin x,
\qquad
\frac{x+1}{x^2+4},
\qquad
(3x^2-1)^7.
\]
The answers are sum, product, quotient, and composition. Those words determine the first rule.
\end{bgcheckpoint}

\section{Rewrite Before Differentiating}
\lessonobjective{Apply the power rule to radicals and reciprocal powers by rewriting them with exponents.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The shortcuts in \emph{Negative and Fractional Powers} do not replace the limit definition. They package conclusions already justified from it. That distinction matters because a rule applies only when the function has the relevant structure and lies in its domain. A familiar-looking exponent or fraction is not permission to differentiate blindly.

After using a rule, check the result structurally. A derivative of a polynomial should have lower degree. A product derivative should usually contain contributions from both factors. A quotient result should preserve the denominator restriction. These checks are quick enough to use on homework and valuable enough to use on exams.
\end{bgexposition}




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Rewrite before differentiating}]
Expressions such as \(1/x^3\) and \(\sqrt[4]{x^7}\) are power functions in disguise. Writing them as \(x^{-3}\) and \(x^{7/4}\) lets the power rule operate without inventing separate rules for every radical and reciprocal.

The rewritten form also exposes domain issues. A derivative formula may be algebraically correct but defined only where the original function and the relevant powers make sense. Calculus answers live on domains, not in a symbol vacuum.
\end{bgexposition}

Radicals and reciprocals are power functions wearing different notation. Rewriting them with rational or negative exponents reveals the structure the power rule needs. This is not cosmetic algebra; it is a way of making the function's architecture visible.

Domains matter more here. A symbolic derivative formula may exist on intervals where the original real-valued function is defined, but not beyond them. For example, \(\sqrt{x}\) and its derivative are real only on appropriate domains, and the derivative becomes unbounded as \(x\to0^+\).

The power rule is easiest to use when every variable factor is written as \(x^n\):
\[
\frac1{x^m}=x^{-m},\qquad \sqrt{x}=x^{1/2},\qquad \sqrt[3]{x^2}=x^{2/3}.
\]

\begin{bgguided}[title={A reciprocal and a square root}]
Differentiate
\[
f(x)=\frac{4}{x^3}-5\sqrt{x}.
\]
\begin{bgsolution}
Rewrite first:
\[
f(x)=4x^{-3}-5x^{1/2}.
\]
Now apply the power rule:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)
&=4(-3)x^{-4}-5\left(\frac12\right)x^{-1/2}\\
&=-12x^{-4}-\frac52x^{-1/2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
A conventional final form is
\[
\boxed{f'(x)=-\frac{12}{x^4}-\frac{5}{2\sqrt{x}}}.
\]
The original function is defined for \(x>0\); the derivative formula also reflects that domain.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={A cube-root power}]
For \(g(x)=\sqrt[3]{x^5}=x^{5/3}\),
\[
g'(x)=\frac53x^{2/3}.
\]
This derivative exists for every real \(x\), including \(0\).
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgexamnote}
Do not rewrite \(1/(x^2+1)\) as \(x^{-2}+1\). A negative exponent applies to the entire base inside its parentheses. The function \((x^2+1)^{-1}\) requires the chain rule, introduced later.
\end{bgexamnote}

\begin{bgexercises}
\item Differentiate \(x^{-7}\).
\item Differentiate \(6/\sqrt{x}\).
\item Differentiate \(3\sqrt[4]{x^3}\).
\item Find the tangent slope of \(f(x)=\sqrt{x}\) at \(x=9\).
\item State the domain on which the derivative of \(x^{2/3}\) is finite.
\end{bgexercises}


\begin{bgapplication}[title={Stopping distance and square-root speed}]
In a simplified braking model, the maximum safe speed on a fixed stopping distance \(d\) may have the form
\[
v(d)=k\sqrt d.
\]
Then
\[
v'(d)=\frac{k}{2\sqrt d}.
\]
Increasing available distance helps most when the original stopping distance is small; the marginal gain decreases as \(d\) grows. The fractional exponent makes that diminishing sensitivity visible.
\end{bgapplication}

\section{Linearity of Differentiation}
\lessonobjective{Use constant-multiple and sum rules; differentiate polynomial and mixed power expressions efficiently.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The shortcuts in \emph{Sums and Constant Multiples} do not replace the limit definition. They package conclusions already justified from it. That distinction matters because a rule applies only when the function has the relevant structure and lies in its domain. A familiar-looking exponent or fraction is not permission to differentiate blindly.

After using a rule, check the result structurally. A derivative of a polynomial should have lower degree. A product derivative should usually contain contributions from both factors. A quotient result should preserve the denominator restriction. These checks are quick enough to use on homework and valuable enough to use on exams.
\end{bgexposition}




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Differentiate a sum piece by piece}]
If an output is built by adding several contributions, a small change in the total is the sum of the small changes in those contributions. That is why derivatives distribute across sums and differences. A constant multiplier simply scales every output change by the same amount, so it scales the derivative too.

This linear behavior is one of the cleanest parts of differentiation. It lets a long polynomial be handled term by term rather than as one giant object. Keep the signs attached to their terms and simplify only after each derivative is correct.
\end{bgexposition}

Many models are built by adding simpler effects: fixed cost plus variable cost, baseline temperature plus oscillation, or several forces acting together. Differentiation respects that addition. Each component contributes its own rate, and a constant multiplier scales the rate by the same amount.

This linearity is why complicated-looking polynomials are routine. It is also why units and interpretation can be handled component by component, provided every term describes the same output quantity.

If \(c\) is constant, then
\[
\frac{d}{dx}[cf(x)]=cf'(x).
\]
If \(f\) and \(g\) are differentiable, then
\[
\frac{d}{dx}[f(x)\pm g(x)]=f'(x)\pm g'(x).
\]
Together these say differentiation is a linear operation:
\[
\frac{d}{dx}[af(x)+bg(x)]=af'(x)+bg'(x).
\]

\begin{bgguided}[title={A mixed power expression}]
Differentiate
\[
y=3x^{7/2}-4x^{-2}+9.
\]
\begin{bgsolution}
Keep the coefficients and apply the power rule separately:
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=3\left(\frac72\right)x^{5/2}-4(-2)x^{-3}+0.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{y'=\frac{21}{2}x^{5/2}+8x^{-3}}.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgproofidea}
The sum rule follows directly from limits because
\[
\frac{(f+g)(x+h)-(f+g)(x)}{h}
=\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}h+\frac{g(x+h)-g(x)}h.
\]
Taking limits separates the sum into \(f'(x)+g'(x)\).
\end{bgproofidea}

\begin{bgcheck}{linearity-01}{expression}{10x^4+6x^-4}[Quick check]
Differentiate \(2x^5-2x^{-3}+8\).
\begin{bgreveal}\(\boxed{10x^4+6x^{-4}}\).\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}


\begin{bgapplication}[title={Total electrical load}]
Suppose three devices draw power
\[
P_1(t)=40+2t,
\quad P_2(t)=25+3t^2,
\quad P_3(t)=10e^{0.1t}.
\]
The total load is \(P=P_1+P_2+P_3\), so
\[
P'(t)=2+6t+e^{0.1t}.
\]
Each device contributes independently to the rate at which the building's total power demand changes. This is linearity in a context where the units remain watts per unit time throughout.
\end{bgapplication}

\section{Products of Changing Functions}
\lessonobjective{Use and explain the product rule; decide when expansion is preferable.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The shortcuts in \emph{The Product Rule} do not replace the limit definition. They package conclusions already justified from it. That distinction matters because a rule applies only when the function has the relevant structure and lies in its domain. A familiar-looking exponent or fraction is not permission to differentiate blindly.

After using a rule, check the result structurally. A derivative of a polynomial should have lower degree. A product derivative should usually contain contributions from both factors. A quotient result should preserve the denominator restriction. These checks are quick enough to use on homework and valuable enough to use on exams.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoAProductRectangle




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Both factors are changing}]
The tempting but false rule \((fg)'=f'g'\) ignores two first-order contributions. When \(x\) changes, the first factor changes while the second still contributes its current size, and the second factor changes while the first contributes its current size. The product rule adds those two effects.

The area model makes this visible: a changing rectangle gains one strip from the width change and another from the height change. The tiny corner where both changes occur is second order and disappears relative to the main strips in the derivative limit.
\end{bgexposition}

When two changing factors are multiplied, both can contribute to the change in the product. Revenue equals price times quantity, electrical power equals voltage times current, and the area of a changing rectangle equals length times width. Differentiating only one factor ignores part of the motion.

The product rule is therefore a bookkeeping law for simultaneous change. One term records the effect of changing the first factor while freezing the second; the other records the effect of changing the second while freezing the first.

The derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives. If both factors change, each contributes to the total change.

\begin{bgtheorem}[title={Product rule}]
\[
\boxed{\frac{d}{dx}[f(x)g(x)]=f'(x)g(x)+f(x)g'(x)}.
\]
A useful spoken form is: derivative of the first times the second, plus the first times derivative of the second.
\end{bgtheorem}

\begin{bgproofidea}[title={The missing term that naive multiplication ignores}]
Add and subtract \(f(x+h)g(x)\) in the product difference quotient. This separates the change into one part caused by \(g\) and one part caused by \(f\). After taking limits, the two surviving contributions are \(f'g\) and \(fg'\). Geometrically, if a rectangle's width and height both change, the added area contains two main strips; multiplying only the derivatives measures neither strip correctly.
\end{bgproofidea}

\begin{bgguided}[title={A polynomial times a radical}]
Differentiate
\[
y=(x^2+1)\sqrt{x}.
\]
\begin{bgsolution}
Name the factors:
\[
u=x^2+1,\qquad v=x^{1/2}.
\]
Then
\[
u'=2x,\qquad v'=\frac12x^{-1/2}.
\]
Apply the product rule:
\[
\begin{aligned}
y'&=u'v+uv'\\
&=2x\sqrt{x}+(x^2+1)\frac1{2\sqrt{x}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is already correct. A common denominator gives
\[
\boxed{y'=\frac{5x^2+1}{2\sqrt{x}}}.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={Expand or use the product rule?}]
For \(y=(x+2)(x^2-3x+1)\), either method works. Expansion produces a polynomial and is likely fastest. For \(y=x^2\sin x\), expansion is impossible, so the product rule is required. Rule choice is part of the mathematics, not clerical decoration.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgmistake}
\[
(fg)'\ne f'g'.
\]
A quick counterexample is \(f(x)=g(x)=x\). The derivative of \(x^2\) is \(2x\), while \(f'g'=1\).
\end{bgmistake}

\begin{bgcheck}{product-rule-01}{expression}{3x^2sin(x)+x^3cos(x)}[Quick check]
Differentiate \(x^3\sin x\).
\begin{bgreveal}\(\boxed{3x^2\sin x+x^3\cos x}\).\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}


\begin{bgmodelinglab}[title={Revenue when price falls as sales rise}]
A vendor expects to sell \(q(t)=200+30t\) units per week after an advertising launch, while the market price falls according to \(p(t)=50-2t\) dollars per unit. Revenue is
\[
R(t)=p(t)q(t).
\]
Therefore
\[
R'(t)=p'(t)q(t)+p(t)q'(t).
\]
At \(t=4\), \(p=42\), \(q=320\), \(p'=-2\), and \(q'=30\). Hence
\[
R'(4)=(-2)(320)+(42)(30)=620\text{ dollars/week}^{2}.
\]
The falling price reduces revenue by \(640\) dollars per week squared, while growing sales add \(1260\); the net effect is positive.
\end{bgmodelinglab}

\begin{bgadvanced}[title={A first glimpse of differentials}]
If \(f\) changes by \(df\) and \(g\) changes by \(dg\), then
\[
(f+df)(g+dg)-fg=g\,df+f\,dg+df\,dg.
\]
The last term is second order: it is the product of two small changes. After dividing by the input change and taking a limit, that second-order contribution disappears, leaving the product rule. This ``keep the first-order terms'' principle becomes central in multivariable calculus and numerical analysis.
\end{bgadvanced}

\section{Quotients of Changing Functions}
\lessonobjective{Use the quotient rule, simplify derivatives, and recognize when negative exponents are easier.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
Treat \emph{The Quotient Rule} as an exercise in decomposition. Circle the largest pieces of the expression and name the operation connecting them. Only then work inward. This approach turns a dense formula into a short tree of decisions and makes nested derivatives manageable.

Do not confuse rewriting with differentiating. Rewriting may reveal an easier power or cancel a legitimate common factor, but every rewrite must preserve the function on the relevant domain. Once the structure is clear, apply the rule, preserve parentheses, and perform a reasonableness check at a convenient input.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoAQuotientContributions




\begin{bgexposition}[title={A quotient changes through its top and its bottom}]
A fraction can change because the numerator changes, because the denominator changes, or because both change at once. The quotient rule tracks these effects with opposite signs: increasing the numerator tends to raise the quotient, while increasing a positive denominator tends to lower it.

Write the rule in a stable verbal order before substituting: bottom times derivative of top, minus top times derivative of bottom, all over bottom squared. Then place parentheses around every composite numerator and denominator before simplifying.
\end{bgexposition}

Ratios appear whenever one quantity is normalized by another: concentration is mass per volume, average cost is total cost per item, and efficiency is useful output per input. If numerator and denominator both change, the rate of the ratio depends on both changes and on the current size of the denominator.

The quotient rule is easy to misremember because its two numerator terms look similar. Rather than chanting a rhyme under exam stress, identify the top and bottom functions, write their derivatives, and assemble the rule in a fixed order.

\begin{bgtheorem}[title={Quotient rule}]
If \(g(x)\ne0\), then
\[
\boxed{\left(\frac{f}{g}\right)'=\frac{f'g-fg'}{g^2}}.
\]
A memory phrase is ``low d-high minus high d-low, over low squared.'' The phrase is ugly but less ugly than losing a sign on an exam.
\end{bgtheorem}

\begin{bgguided}[title={Differentiate a rational function}]
Differentiate
\[
y=\frac{x^2+1}{x-3}.
\]
\begin{bgsolution}
Let the numerator be \(f=x^2+1\) and denominator be \(g=x-3\). Then
\[
f'=2x,\qquad g'=1.
\]
Apply the rule in the correct order:
\[
\begin{aligned}
y'&=\frac{(2x)(x-3)-(x^2+1)(1)}{(x-3)^2}\\
&=\frac{2x^2-6x-x^2-1}{(x-3)^2}\\
&=\boxed{\frac{x^2-6x-1}{(x-3)^2}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The derivative is defined only where the original quotient is defined, so \(x\ne3\).
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={When the quotient rule is unnecessary}]
For
\[
y=\frac{3x^4-2x}{x^2}=3x^2-2x^{-1},
\]
simplify first and use the power rule:
\[
y'=6x+2x^{-2}.
\]
This is safer than applying the quotient rule to an expression that readily simplifies.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgmistake}
The numerator order matters. Swapping \(f'g-fg'\) to \(fg'-f'g\) changes the sign of the entire derivative.
\end{bgmistake}

\begin{bgcheck}{quotient-rule-01}{expression}{(1-x^2)/(x^2+1)^2}[Quick check]
Differentiate \(x/(x^2+1)\).
\begin{bgreveal}
\[
\frac{(1)(x^2+1)-x(2x)}{(x^2+1)^2}
=\boxed{\frac{1-x^2}{(x^2+1)^2}}.
\]
\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}


\begin{bgmodelinglab}[title={Average production cost}]
A workshop's total daily cost for \(q\) units is
\[
C(q)=1200+18q+0.02q^2.
\]
Average cost is
\[
A(q)=\frac{C(q)}q=\frac{1200}{q}+18+0.02q.
\]
Differentiating the simplified form gives
\[
A'(q)=-\frac{1200}{q^2}+0.02.
\]
At \(q=100\), \(A'(100)=-0.10\) dollar per item per additional item. Near that output, producing one additional unit lowers average cost by about ten cents because fixed cost is being spread more widely.
\end{bgmodelinglab}

\section{Read Structure Before Calculating}
\lessonobjective{Identify the outermost operation and select an efficient differentiation strategy.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
Treat \emph{How to Choose a Differentiation Rule} as an exercise in decomposition. Circle the largest pieces of the expression and name the operation connecting them. Only then work inward. This approach turns a dense formula into a short tree of decisions and makes nested derivatives manageable.

Do not confuse rewriting with differentiating. Rewriting may reveal an easier power or cancel a legitimate common factor, but every rewrite must preserve the function on the relevant domain. Once the structure is clear, apply the rule, preserve parentheses, and perform a reasonableness check at a convenient input.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoARuleSelection




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Read the outermost operation first}]
Rule selection is a structure-reading skill. Ask what operation is performed last. If two large expressions are multiplied, start with the product rule. If one expression is substituted inside another, start with the chain rule. If the whole expression is a sum, separate the terms first.

A complicated formula often uses several rules, but only one rule governs the outer layer. Marking that layer before calculating prevents the common mistake of applying a familiar rule to the wrong part of the expression.
\end{bgexposition}

Differentiation becomes difficult when students start calculating before they have read the expression. The decisive question is not ``which symbols do I see?'' but ``what is the outermost operation?'' A product at the top level needs the product rule even if one factor contains a composition; a composition at the top level needs the chain rule even if the inner function is a quotient.

Treat rule selection like parsing a sentence. Parentheses, fraction bars, powers, and function names reveal which parts belong together. A ten-second structural scan can save several minutes of algebraic archaeology.

\begin{bgdecision}[title={Rule-selection flow}]
\begin{enumerate}
\item Simplify harmless algebra first: combine powers, cancel common factors where valid, and rewrite radicals.
\item Identify the outermost operation joining variable expressions.
\item If it is addition or subtraction, differentiate term by term.
\item If it is multiplication, use expansion when short or the product rule when expansion is impossible or cumbersome.
\item If it is division, simplify first; otherwise use the quotient rule.
\item If one function is placed inside another, the chain rule will also be required.
\end{enumerate}
\end{bgdecision}

Compare:
\[
(x^2+1)(x^3-2),\qquad \frac{x^2+1}{x^3-2},\qquad (x^2+1)^5.
\]
The visible symbols may look similar, but their outer operations are product, quotient, and composition. They require different rules.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Name the rule before taking the derivative}]
Choose the primary rule for each expression.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item \(x^4+3x^{-2}\)
\item \((x^2+1)\cos x\)
\item \((x+1)/(x^2+4)\)
\item \((3x-2)^7\)
\end{enumerate}
\begin{bgsolution}
(a) Sum and power rules. (b) Product rule. (c) Quotient rule. (d) Chain rule because a seventh power is applied to the inner function \(3x-2\).
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexercises}
\item Differentiate \((x^2+3)(x^3-x)\) by expansion and by the product rule; verify the forms agree.
\item Differentiate \((2x+1)/(x^2+1)\).
\item Simplify and differentiate \((x^3+x)/x\).
\item Explain why \((x^2+1)^4\) cannot be differentiated by simply applying the power rule to \(x\).
\end{bgexercises}

\chapter{Trigonometric, Exponential, and Logarithmic Derivatives}
\section{The Derivatives of \(\sin x\) and \(\cos x\)}
\lessonobjective{Differentiate sine and cosine; understand how the fundamental trigonometric limits produce the rules.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
Special-function derivatives become less mysterious in \emph{Derivatives of Sine and Cosine} when you connect them to inverses and limits. The derivative of $\ln x$ follows from its inverse relationship with $e^x$; the derivative of tangent follows from sine, cosine, and the quotient rule. Learning these connections reduces memorization and provides recovery routes when a formula is forgotten.

Use a graph or a numerical point to check signs and scale. If the function is increasing rapidly, its derivative should be positive and large. If the function is undefined at an input, its derivative formula cannot rescue that input.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoATrigPhase




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Trigonometric derivatives describe circular motion}]
Sine and cosine are not arbitrary special cases. They are coordinates of motion around a unit circle. As a point moves, the horizontal and vertical coordinates trade roles in a quarter-turn pattern, which is why differentiation cycles through \(\sin x\), \(\cos x\), \(-\sin x\), and \(-\cos x\).

Angles must be measured in radians for the clean derivative formulas to hold. Radians connect arc length directly to angle, allowing the limit \(\sin h/h\to1\) to produce derivatives with no conversion constant.
\end{bgexposition}

Sine and cosine are not polynomial decorations. They encode periodic motion: rotations, waves, seasons, vibrations, and repeating signals. Their derivatives swap the two functions, with a negative sign appearing for cosine because cosine is decreasing at the origin while sine is increasing.

The familiar formulas require radians. Radian measure makes arc length directly proportional to angle, allowing the local ratio \(\sin h/h\) to approach \(1\). Degree measure inserts an unwanted conversion factor into every derivative.

Angles must be measured in radians for the standard derivative formulas.

\begin{bgtheorem}[title={Sine and cosine derivatives}]
\[
\boxed{\frac{d}{dx}\sin x=\cos x},
\qquad
\boxed{\frac{d}{dx}\cos x=-\sin x}.
\]
\end{bgtheorem}

\begin{bgproofidea}[title={Why the derivative of sine is cosine}]
Start from
\[
\frac{\sin(x+h)-\sin x}{h}.
\]
Use \(\sin(x+h)=\sin x\cos h+\cos x\sin h\):
\[
\sin x\frac{\cos h-1}{h}+\cos x\frac{\sin h}{h}.
\]
As \(h\to0\), the first quotient approaches \(0\) and the second approaches \(1\). The limit is \(\cos x\). The cosine proof uses the angle-addition identity and yields \(-\sin x\).
\end{bgproofidea}

\begin{bgguided}[title={Differentiate a trigonometric polynomial}]
Differentiate
\[
f(x)=3\sin x-4\cos x+x^3.
\]
\begin{bgsolution}
Use linearity and the three basic derivative rules:
\[
\frac{d}{dx}[3\sin x]=3\cos x,
\]
\[
\frac{d}{dx}[-4\cos x]=4\sin x,
\]
\[
\frac{d}{dx}[x^3]=3x^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{f'(x)=3\cos x+4\sin x+3x^2}.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={A tangent line to sine}]
At \(x=\pi/3\), \(y=\sin x\) has point
\[
\left(\frac\pi3,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)
\]
and slope
\[
\cos\frac\pi3=\frac12.
\]
Thus the tangent line is
\[
\boxed{y-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=\frac12\left(x-\frac\pi3\right)}.
\]
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgcheck}{sin-cos-01}{expression}{4cos(x)-2sin(x)}[Quick check]
Differentiate \(4\sin x+2\cos x\).
\begin{bgreveal}\(\boxed{4\cos x-2\sin x}\).\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}


\begin{bgmodelinglab}[title={Vertical velocity on a Ferris wheel}]
A rider's height is
\[
h(t)=22-18\cos\left(\frac{\pi t}{20}\right)
\]
meters, where one revolution takes \(40\) seconds. Then
\[
h'(t)=\frac{18\pi}{20}\sin\left(\frac{\pi t}{20}\right).
\]
At \(t=10\), the rider is halfway up the first ascent and
\[
h'(10)=\frac{9\pi}{10}\text{ m/s}.
\]
At the bottom and top, the derivative is zero because the rider's vertical direction reverses, even though the wheel never stops rotating.
\end{bgmodelinglab}

\begin{bgadvanced}[title={Why radians are mathematically natural}]
For an angle \(h\) in radians on the unit circle, the arc length is exactly \(h\). This geometric identity leads to \(\sin h/h\to1\). If the angle is measured in degrees, the arc length is \(\pi h/180\), and the derivative of \(\sin h\) acquires the factor \(\pi/180\). Radians are not a convention chosen to annoy students; they are the coordinate in which circular motion has unit local scale.
\end{bgadvanced}

\section{Tangent, Cotangent, Secant, and Cosecant}
\lessonobjective{Differentiate all six trigonometric functions and connect the rules to quotient and product identities.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
In \emph{Derivatives of the Other Trigonometric Functions}, begin by asking what the original function does. Where does it rise, fall, flatten, or grow in proportion to itself? The derivative formula should match that qualitative behavior. A missing minus sign in the cosine derivative, for example, contradicts the fact that cosine decreases immediately to the right of zero.

When several special functions appear together, separate recognition from computation. Identify each basic derivative, note any composition requiring the chain rule, and then combine the pieces. A short verbal plan keeps a crowded formula from becoming a guessing contest.
\end{bgexposition}




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Build the remaining trig derivatives from sine and cosine}]
Tangent, cotangent, secant, and cosecant do not require four unrelated derivations. Rewrite them using sine and cosine, then use quotient or product rules. The resulting formulas inherit both the geometry of the unit circle and the algebra of reciprocals.

Domain restrictions matter. A formula involving \(\sec x\) is meaningful only where \(\cos x\neq0\), and the derivative cannot repair a point where the original function is undefined.
\end{bgexposition}

The remaining trigonometric derivatives do not need six unrelated proofs. Tangent and cotangent are quotients; secant and cosecant are reciprocals. The product and quotient rules, together with the Pythagorean identities, generate the entire table.

Rebuilding a forgotten formula from identities is slower than perfect memory but much faster than inventing a sign. It also explains where the domain restrictions come from: a trigonometric derivative cannot be used where the original function is undefined.

Using \(\tan x=\sin x/\cos x\) and the quotient rule gives
\[
\frac{d}{dx}\tan x=\sec^2x.
\]
The complete table is
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{function}&\text{derivative}\\\hline
\sin x&\cos x\\
\cos x&-\sin x\\
\tan x&\sec^2x\\
\cot x&-\csc^2x\\
\sec x&\sec x\tan x\\
\csc x&-\csc x\cot x
\end{array}
\]

\begin{bgmethod}[title={A sign pattern worth understanding}]
The cofunctions beginning with the letter ``c'' are not all negative. The negative rules are cosine, cotangent, and cosecant. Secant is positive. It is better to rebuild a forgotten rule from identities than to rely on a panicked chant.
\end{bgmethod}

\begin{bgguided}[title={Differentiate a quotient containing tangent}]
Differentiate
\[
y=\frac{\tan x}{x^2}.
\]
\begin{bgsolution}
Use the quotient rule with \(f=\tan x\), \(g=x^2\):
\[
f'=\sec^2x,\qquad g'=2x.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
y'
&=\frac{x^2\sec^2x-(\tan x)(2x)}{x^4}\\
&=\boxed{\frac{x\sec^2x-2\tan x}{x^3}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={Differentiate a secant product}]
\[
\frac{d}{dx}[x\sec x]=\sec x+x\sec x\tan x.
\]
Both terms are required by the product rule.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgexercises}
\item Differentiate \(5\tan x-2\cot x\).
\item Differentiate \(x^2\csc x\).
\item Differentiate \(\sec x/(x+1)\).
\item Find the tangent line to \(y=\tan x\) at \(x=\pi/4\).
\end{bgexercises}

\section{Why \(e^x\) Is the Natural Exponential}
\lessonobjective{Differentiate \(e^x\); interpret exponential self-proportional growth.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The formulas in \emph{The Derivative of the Natural Exponential} are easiest to remember when connected to graph behavior. Trigonometric derivatives encode phase and sign patterns, exponential derivatives encode proportional growth, and logarithmic derivatives encode reciprocal sensitivity. The formulas are not unrelated entries in a table.

Keep domain and units visible. Trigonometric derivative formulas use radians. Logarithms require positive real inputs unless a different domain has been explicitly introduced. General exponential and logarithmic bases contribute constants such as $\ln a$. These details are small on the page and decisive in a correct solution.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoAExpTangent




\begin{bgexposition}[title={The function whose slope matches its height}]
Most functions change shape when differentiated. The natural exponential is exceptional: at every input, the tangent slope equals the function value. A height of \(5\) comes with slope \(5\); a height of \(1/2\) comes with slope \(1/2\).

This self-reproducing behavior is why \(e^x\) appears in continuous growth, radioactive decay, cooling, finance, and differential equations. The same rule describes growth and decay; the sign in the exponent determines the direction.
\end{bgexposition}

Most functions change at a rate different from their current size. The natural exponential is special because it reproduces itself under differentiation:
\[
\frac{d}{dx}e^x=e^x.
\]
That property makes \(e^x\) the natural language of continuous growth and decay.

Whenever the rate of change is proportional to the amount present, exponential functions appear. Populations, radioactive samples, continuously compounded balances, and idealized drug elimination all share this mathematical skeleton even though their physical stories differ.

The number \(e\) is the unique positive base whose exponential function has slope equal to height everywhere.

\begin{bgtheorem}[title={Derivative of the natural exponential}]
\[
\boxed{\frac{d}{dx}e^x=e^x}.
\]
\end{bgtheorem}

From the definition,
\[
\frac{e^{x+h}-e^x}{h}=e^x\frac{e^h-1}{h}.
\]
The base \(e\) is characterized by
\[
\lim_{h\to0}\frac{e^h-1}{h}=1.
\]
Therefore the derivative is \(e^x\).

\begin{bgguided}[title={Differentiate a polynomial-exponential product}]
Differentiate
\[
f(x)=x^2e^x.
\]
\begin{bgsolution}
This is a product of \(x^2\) and \(e^x\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)
&=(2x)e^x+x^2e^x\\
&=\boxed{e^x(x^2+2x)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Factoring \(e^x\) is optional but useful for later sign analysis because \(e^x>0\).
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgconcept}[title={Rate proportional to amount}]
If \(P(t)=Ce^{kt}\), then \(P'(t)=kP(t)\). The quantity changes at a rate proportional to its current amount. This pattern appears in population models, continuous interest, cooling approximations, and radioactive decay.
\end{bgconcept}

\begin{bgcheck}{exp-e-01}{expression}{e^x(x+1)}[Quick check]
Differentiate \(xe^x\).
\begin{bgreveal}\(\boxed{e^x+xe^x=e^x(x+1)}\).\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}


\begin{bgapplication}[title={Continuous bacterial growth}]
A culture is modeled by
\[
P(t)=800e^{0.35t}.
\]
Then
\[
P'(t)=0.35P(t).
\]
The culture grows at \(35\%\) of its current size per hour. When \(P=2000\), the instantaneous growth rate is \(700\) cells per hour, regardless of which time produced that population. Exponential models tie rate directly to current amount.
\end{bgapplication}

\begin{bgadvanced}[title={Characterizing the exponential by its derivative}]
The differential equation \(y'=y\) with initial condition \(y(0)=1\) has the unique solution \(y=e^x\). In analysis, this can be used as a definition of the natural exponential. The function is not merely one convenient growth model; it is the unique function whose local proportional growth rate is constantly one.
\end{bgadvanced}

\section{Bases Other Than \(e\)}
\lessonobjective{Differentiate \(a^x\) and explain the role of \(\ln a\).}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
In \emph{Derivatives of General Exponential Functions}, begin by asking what the original function does. Where does it rise, fall, flatten, or grow in proportion to itself? The derivative formula should match that qualitative behavior. A missing minus sign in the cosine derivative, for example, contradicts the fact that cosine decreases immediately to the right of zero.

When several special functions appear together, separate recognition from computation. Identify each basic derivative, note any composition requiring the chain rule, and then combine the pieces. A short verbal plan keeps a crowded formula from becoming a guessing contest.
\end{bgexposition}




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Other bases carry a growth-rate constant}]
A function \(a^x\) grows by the same percentage for equal input changes, but its instantaneous relative growth rate is \(\ln a\), not always one. Writing \(a^x=e^{x\ln a}\) exposes the chain rule and explains the derivative \(a^x\ln a\).

For \(0<a<1\), \(\ln a<0\), so the derivative is negative. The formula therefore encodes the difference between exponential growth and exponential decay automatically.
\end{bgexposition}

A base such as \(2\), \(10\), or \(1.03\) changes the scale of exponential growth. The factor \(\ln a\) in
\[
\frac{d}{dx}a^x=a^x\ln a
\]
measures how aggressive that base is. Bases above \(1\) give positive rates; bases between \(0\) and \(1\) give negative rates.

The formula becomes especially useful when the exponent is itself a function. Then the exponential rule and chain rule work together, separating the current amount from the rate at which the exponent changes.

For \(a>0\), write
\[
a^x=e^{x\ln a}.
\]
The chain rule, developed fully in the next section, gives
\[
\boxed{\frac{d}{dx}a^x=a^x\ln a}.
\]
The factor \(\ln a\) measures how rapidly the chosen base grows relative to \(e\).

\begin{bgguided}[title={Differentiate a base-2 exponential}]
Differentiate \(f(x)=3\cdot2^x\).
\begin{bgsolution}
The constant \(3\) remains, and
\[
\frac{d}{dx}2^x=2^x\ln2.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{f'(x)=3\cdot2^x\ln2}.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={Exponential decay base}]
For \(g(t)=5(0.8)^t\),
\[
g'(t)=5(0.8)^t\ln(0.8).
\]
Since \(\ln(0.8)<0\), the derivative is negative, matching decay.
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgmistake}
The power rule does not apply to \(2^x\). In \(x^n\), the variable is the base. In \(a^x\), the variable is the exponent. Those are different structures.
\end{bgmistake}


\begin{bgapplication}[title={A depreciating device}]
A device worth \(V(t)=2400(0.82)^t\) dollars after \(t\) years has derivative
\[
V'(t)=2400(0.82)^t\ln(0.82).
\]
At purchase, \(V'(0)=2400\ln(0.82)\approx-476\) dollars per year. The derivative becomes less negative over time because the same percentage decline acts on a smaller remaining value.
\end{bgapplication}

\section{The Natural Logarithm}
\lessonobjective{Differentiate \(\ln x\) and \(\ln|x|\); connect the rule to inverse functions.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
Special-function derivatives become less mysterious in \emph{The Derivative of the Natural Logarithm} when you connect them to inverses and limits. The derivative of $\ln x$ follows from its inverse relationship with $e^x$; the derivative of tangent follows from sine, cosine, and the quotient rule. Learning these connections reduces memorization and provides recovery routes when a formula is forgotten.

Use a graph or a numerical point to check signs and scale. If the function is increasing rapidly, its derivative should be positive and large. If the function is undefined at an input, its derivative formula cannot rescue that input.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoALogInverse




\begin{bgexposition}[title={The logarithm measures how much exponent is needed}]
Because \(\ln x\) reverses \(e^x\), its slope must undo the exponential slope. At the point \((x,\ln x)\), the inverse point is \((\ln x,x)\) on \(e^x\), whose slope is \(x\). Reflection across \(y=x\) turns that slope into its reciprocal \(1/x\).

The derivative becomes smaller as \(x\) grows, matching the graph: equal multiplicative changes in \(x\) produce equal additive changes in \(\ln x\), so large absolute changes matter less at larger scales.
\end{bgexposition}

The natural logarithm is the inverse of the natural exponential, but its derivative also has a direct geometric meaning: \(1/x\) measures the relative effect of a fixed additive change at different scales. Adding one unit matters enormously near zero and barely matters when \(x\) is huge.

This scale sensitivity is why logarithms appear in sound levels, information, growth comparisons, and elasticity. The domain restriction \(x>0\) is part of the function, not a technical footnote to be remembered only after losing points.

Because \(y=\ln x\) is the inverse of \(x=e^y\), its derivative is the reciprocal of the derivative of \(e^y\):
\[
\boxed{\frac{d}{dx}\ln x=\frac1x},\qquad x>0.
\]
More generally,
\[
\boxed{\frac{d}{dx}\ln|x|=\frac1x},\qquad x\ne0.
\]

\begin{bgguided}[title={Differentiate a logarithmic product}]
Differentiate
\[
f(x)=x^2\ln x,
\qquad x>0.
\]
\begin{bgsolution}
Use the product rule:
\[
\begin{aligned}
f'(x)
&=(2x)\ln x+x^2\left(\frac1x\right)\\
&=\boxed{2x\ln x+x}.
\end{aligned}
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={A logarithm of an absolute value}]
For \(f(x)=\ln|x-4|\), the chain rule gives
\[
f'(x)=\frac1{x-4},\qquad x\ne4.
\]
The absolute value allows the logarithm to be defined on both sides of \(4\).
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgcheck}{ln-01}{expression}{2xln(x)+x}[Quick check]
Differentiate \(x^2\ln x\).
\begin{bgreveal}\(\boxed{2x\ln x+x}\).\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}


\begin{bgapplication}[title={Diminishing benefit from study time}]
Suppose a rough mastery score follows
\[
M(t)=60+12\ln(1+t),
\]
where \(t\) is focused study time in hours. Then
\[
M'(t)=\frac{12}{1+t}.
\]
The model predicts large early gains and smaller later gains. At \(t=1\), the marginal gain is \(6\) score units per hour; at \(t=5\), it is \(2\). This is diminishing return, not an argument to stop studying after one hour, however eagerly the algebra may be misquoted.
\end{bgapplication}

\begin{bgadvanced}[title={The logarithm as accumulated reciprocal growth}]
A later integration unit will define
\[
\ln x=\int_1^x\frac{1}{t}\,dt.
\]
The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus then gives \((\ln x)'=1/x\) immediately. This connects logarithms to area, multiplicative scaling, and the fact that equal percentage changes correspond to equal logarithmic differences.
\end{bgadvanced}

\section{Logarithms with Any Positive Base}
\lessonobjective{Differentiate \(\log_a x\) and use change of base.}

\begin{bgbridge}[title={Base changes scale, not the basic reciprocal shape}]
At the same positive input, every logarithm has a derivative proportional to $1/x$. The factor $1/\ln a$ stretches the slope vertically. Bases larger than one give positive slopes; bases between zero and one give negative slopes. This lets a graph check the sign of a symbolic answer before any algebra is simplified.
\end{bgbridge}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
The formulas in \emph{Derivatives of General Logarithms} are easiest to remember when connected to graph behavior. Trigonometric derivatives encode phase and sign patterns, exponential derivatives encode proportional growth, and logarithmic derivatives encode reciprocal sensitivity. The formulas are not unrelated entries in a table.

Keep domain and units visible. Trigonometric derivative formulas use radians. Logarithms require positive real inputs unless a different domain has been explicitly introduced. General exponential and logarithmic bases contribute constants such as $\ln a$. These details are small on the page and decisive in a correct solution.
\end{bgexposition}




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Change the base before differentiating}]
Every logarithm can be written as a constant multiple of the natural logarithm. Since constants pass through differentiation, \(\log_a x\) inherits the derivative of \(\ln x\) with a scale factor \(1/\ln a\).

This is a useful example of mathematical economy: one well-understood function and one algebraic identity replace a separate derivative rule for every possible base.
\end{bgexposition}

Changing the logarithm base changes only a constant scale factor. Because
\[
\log_a x=\frac{\ln x}{\ln a},
\]
all logarithmic derivatives reduce to the natural-log rule. This is another example of calculus rewarding algebraic structure instead of brute-force memorization.

A derivative written in terms of \(1/x\) should be interpreted carefully near zero. The rate becomes large because logarithmic outputs change rapidly when their positive input is small.

For \(a>0\), \(a\ne1\),
\[
\log_a x=\frac{\ln x}{\ln a}.
\]
Since \(\ln a\) is a constant,
\[
\boxed{\frac{d}{dx}\log_a x=\frac1{x\ln a}}.
\]

\begin{bgguided}[title={Differentiate a common logarithm}]
Differentiate \(f(x)=\log_{10}x\).
\begin{bgsolution}
Use the general rule with \(a=10\):
\[
\boxed{f'(x)=\frac1{x\ln10}}.
\]
The derivative is positive for \(x>0\), so the common logarithm is increasing.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={A base less than one}]
If \(0<a<1\), then \(\ln a<0\). Therefore \(1/(x\ln a)<0\), which correctly shows that \(\log_a x\) is decreasing.
\end{bgexample}

\section{Differentiate the Outside, Then the Inside}
\lessonobjective{Apply the chain rule to powers of linear and polynomial inner functions.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
In \emph{The Basic Chain Rule}, the phrase ``outside to inside'' is useful only when paired with structure. Keep the inner expression unchanged while differentiating the outer layer, then multiply by the derivative of that inner expression. If the inner expression is itself composite, continue inward.

A missing inner derivative is the signature chain-rule error. Check units or scaling to catch it. If an inner quantity changes three times as fast, the final output rate should reflect that factor of three. The chain rule is a rate-conversion law, not punctuation attached to parentheses.
\end{bgexposition}




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Differentiate the outside, keep the inside, then multiply by the inside rate}]
The phrase ``outside times inside'' is incomplete. The precise move is: differentiate the outer function while leaving its input placeholder unchanged, then multiply by the derivative of the inner function. For \((g(x))^n\), this gives \(n(g(x))^{n-1}g'(x)\).

Check the result by asking whether every changing layer contributed a factor. If the inner expression is not simply \(x\), an inner derivative should usually appear somewhere in the answer.
\end{bgexposition}

The phrase ``differentiate the outside, keep the inside, multiply by the derivative of the inside'' is a useful first algorithm, but it should not become empty choreography. The inner derivative is present because a one-unit change in \(x\) need not produce a one-unit change in the inner expression.

Before differentiating, name the inner function mentally. If \(y=(3x^2+1)^5\), then the outer power reacts to changes in \(u=3x^2+1\), while \(u\) reacts to changes in \(x\). The chain rule connects the two reactions.

\begin{bgtheorem}[title={Chain rule}]
If \(y=F(u)\) and \(u=g(x)\), then
\[
\boxed{\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{dF}{du}\frac{du}{dx}}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{(F\circ g)'(x)=F'(g(x))g'(x)}.
\]
\end{bgtheorem}

\begin{bgguided}[title={A power of a linear function}]
Differentiate
\[
y=(3x-2)^5.
\]
\begin{bgsolution}
The outer function is a fifth power. Differentiate the outside while leaving the inside unchanged:
\[
5(3x-2)^4.
\]
Now multiply by the derivative of the inside:
\[
\frac{d}{dx}(3x-2)=3.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{y'=15(3x-2)^4}.
\]
A useful verbal pattern is: bring down the outer exponent, keep the inner expression, reduce the outer exponent, then multiply by the derivative of the inner expression.
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgexample}[title={A polynomial inside a reciprocal power}]
\[
y=(x^2+4)^{-3}.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
y'&=-3(x^2+4)^{-4}(2x)\\
&=\boxed{-\frac{6x}{(x^2+4)^4}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
\end{bgexample}

\begin{bgproofidea}[title={Why rates multiply}]
For small changes,
\[
\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}
=\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta u}\frac{\Delta u}{\Delta x}.
\]
As the changes shrink, the two ratios approach \(dy/du\) and \(du/dx\). The chain rule is the exact limit version of multiplying conversion rates through an intermediate variable.
\end{bgproofidea}

\begin{bgcheck}{chain-basic-01}{expression}{12(4x+1)^2}[Quick check]
Differentiate \((4x+1)^3\).
\begin{bgreveal}\(\boxed{12(4x+1)^2}\).\end{bgreveal}
\end{bgcheck}


\begin{bgmodelinglab}[title={A calibrated temperature sensor}]
A sensor produces voltage
\[
V(T)=0.02T^2+0.5T
\]
when temperature is \(T\) degrees Celsius. A display converts voltage to a reading
\[
R(V)=100\sqrt{V}.
\]
The display sensitivity to temperature is
\[
\frac{dR}{dT}=\frac{dR}{dV}\frac{dV}{dT}
=\frac{50}{\sqrt V}(0.04T+0.5).
\]
At a chosen temperature, first compute \(V(T)\), then evaluate the product. The chain rule separates sensor physics from display calibration.
\end{bgmodelinglab}

\begin{bgadvanced}[title={Analysis preview: composition of linear maps}]
Near \(x=a\), suppose \(g\) behaves like
\[
g(a+h)\approx g(a)+g'(a)h.
\]
Near \(g(a)\), suppose \(f\) behaves like
\[
f(g(a)+k)\approx f(g(a))+f'(g(a))k.
\]
Substituting the first local model into the second makes the total linear coefficient
\[
f'(g(a))g'(a).
\]
In multivariable calculus, the same idea becomes matrix multiplication of derivative maps.
\end{bgadvanced}

\section{Peeling a Composite Function Layer by Layer}
\lessonobjective{Differentiate functions with three or more nested layers without losing factors.}

\begin{bgexposition}[title={Before the formulas}]
Composition is the hidden architecture of \emph{Multiple Chain-Rule Layers}. An expression may look like one formula while actually containing several function machines. Draw or list the stages before differentiating. This is especially important when product, quotient, and chain rules appear together, because the outer algebraic connection and the inner compositions must both be respected.

Do not simplify away useful structure too early. A factored derivative often shows each chain factor more clearly and is easier to verify. Simplify after the calculus unless rewriting first genuinely reduces the number of rules required.
\end{bgexposition}

\BGVTwoAChainLayers




\begin{bgexposition}[title={Deep nesting is bookkeeping, not a new theorem}]
A function with four nested layers uses the same chain rule as a function with two. The only challenge is keeping the layers in order. Work from the outside inward and write one derivative factor per layer.

A useful self-check is dimensional: each factor should describe the rate of one stage with respect to the previous stage. When multiplied, intermediate quantities cancel, leaving final-output units per original-input unit.
\end{bgexposition}

Compositions can be nested several layers deep. The safest method is to work from the outside inward, multiplying by one derivative for each layer crossed. Parentheses are not clutter here; they are a map of the dependency chain.

A useful self-check is to count layers before you begin. If a function has three genuine compositions, a correct derivative normally contains three derivative factors unless some simplify to constants.

For a composition \(F(G(H(x)))\), the derivative is
\[
F'(G(H(x)))G'(H(x))H'(x).
\]
Work from the outside inward and multiply one derivative factor for every changing layer.

\begin{bgguided}[title={Three nested layers}]
Differentiate
\[
y=\sqrt{1+(2x-3)^4}.
\]
\begin{bgsolution}
Rewrite the square root as a power:
\[
y=[1+(2x-3)^4]^{1/2}.
\]
The layers are:
\[
\text{square-root power}\quad\to\quad 1+u^4\quad\to\quad u=2x-3.
\]
Differentiate the outer layer:
\[
\frac12[1+(2x-3)^4]^{-1/2}.
\]
Differentiate the middle layer:
\[
4(2x-3)^3.
\]
Differentiate the inner layer:
\[
2.
\]
Multiply:
\[
\boxed{y'=\frac{4(2x-3)^3}{\sqrt{1+(2x-3)^4}}}.
\]
\end{bgsolution}
\end{bgguided}

\begin{bgmethod}[title={Layer audit}]
After differentiating, underline each nontrivial nested layer in the original expression and match it to one factor in the derivative. Missing inner derivatives are the chain-rule version of leaving luggage at the airport.
\end{bgmethod}

\begin{bgexercises}
\item Differentiate \([1+(x^2+1)^3]^4\).
\item Differentiate \(\sqrt{2+\sqrt{x}}\).
\item Differentiate \((1-(3x+2)^5)^{-2}\).
\end{bgexercises}
